keyTakeaways: SurtitleLive began from a playwright's cross-language problem, not from a software category: how can a performance keep its original language while another audience follows it?
English surtitles should work as an invitation into a non-English performance, not as a replacement for the voice, rhythm, and cultural memory of the original language.
Translation as hospitality means designing language routes so more people can meet the work without asking the work to become less itself.
Mobile language choice lets one live performance support English-speaking audiences, original-language readers, and additional prepared language tracks without crowding one shared screen.
Quiet technology supports the stage workflow: prepared text, reviewed language choices, live cueing, mobile viewers, Projection Mode, and recovery when the performance changes.

faq.question: What does "translation as hospitality" mean for theatre?
faq.answer: Translation as hospitality means giving audiences a real way into a performance without asking the original language to disappear. English surtitles can help people follow the story while the spoken or sung language remains alive on stage.

faq.question: Why should English surtitles not replace the original language?
faq.answer: The original language carries rhythm, register, timing, cultural memory, humour, silence, and social pressure. A translation can guide the audience, but the performance loses something if the source language is treated as packaging rather than part of the artwork.

faq.question: How can mobile language choice protect the original voice?
faq.answer: Mobile viewers let each audience member choose an enabled language on their own device. That means English-speaking audiences can read English, original-language readers can keep the source text visible, and invited guests or touring partners can follow another prepared language when the company supports it.

faq.question: Why does live cueing still matter if the surtitles are prepared?
faq.answer: Theatre is not playback. Actors pause, lines change, scenes jump, and timing breathes differently from rehearsal. A human operator can hold, advance, recover, or hide prepared surtitles so the language support follows the live event.

faq.question: Is this an accessibility argument or a marketing argument?
faq.answer: It is both, but it starts from care. Clear language routes can help more people feel able to choose a non-English show, including local audiences, reviewers, programmers, source-language communities, and multilingual visitors.

faq.question: Where can I find the practical setup guide for Fringe surtitles?
faq.answer: For the step-by-step workflow, read Blog 9: How to Add English Surtitles to a Non-English Show at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival. This article explains why the workflow matters artistically; Blog 9 explains how to prepare and run it.

glossary.definition: A way of designing translation and surtitles so audiences can enter a work without forcing the original language or cultural voice to disappear.
The rhythm, register, timing, humour, silence, social pressure, and cultural memory carried by the language in which a performance was made.
A chosen path into a live performance, such as English surtitles, original-language text, or another prepared language track.
Prepared English text shown during a live performance to help audiences follow work spoken or sung in another language.
A browser-based audience view opened by QR code or link, allowing each audience member to read an enabled surtitle language on their own device.
A surtitle display mode intended for a theatre screen or projector, often used alongside mobile viewers when the venue supports projection.
The live process of advancing prepared surtitles in time with the performance, including holding, jumping, or hiding text when the show changes.
